summary: The note examines how recent minimum wage increases, beginning after September 1, 2023, affect employment patterns. It draws on BLS data, economist interviews and business owner surveys to show slight employment growth declines in fast-food, redistributed hours, more part-time roles, automation investment and ripple effects on wages above the minimum. Effects vary by region and business size, and longitudinal studies suggest initial shocks may level off, though long-term outcomes remain hard to predict.
one_line: Analysis of how minimum wage hikes since late 2023 reshape employment, hours, full-time versus part-time mix, automation and wages across sectors and regions.
key_facts: Minimum wage legislation increases have been enacted gradually in several regions, commencing after September 1, 2023.
Some areas have seen minimum wage increases of more than 30% over previous levels.
As of late 2023, Seattle, San Francisco, and New York City have breached the $15 per hour mark.
BLS data shows the fast-food industry, which traditionally pays around the minimum wage, has had a slight decline in employment growth rates.
Technology and professional services have remained largely unaffected in employment numbers by minimum wage increases.
Preliminary findings suggest an uptick in workers over age 25 employed in minimum-wage-paying jobs.

Businesses are redistributing hours among staff to mitigate payroll load; John Havens, a small business owner in Chicago, said he hasn't reduced headcount but has cut some hours and streamlined operations.

Dr. Sarah Lin, a professor of economics at the University of California, said a minimum wage rise often accelerates investment in technology, leading to a more efficient, albeit sometimes smaller, workforce.
Companies are offering more part-time roles and fewer full-time positions to manage increased labor costs, per BLS data.
Workers earning slightly above the new minimum see wage bumps as employers adjust pay scales to maintain wage hierarchies.
Urban areas with higher costs of living and greater economic diversity absorb wage increases more readily than rural areas.
Larger corporations with better economies of scale respond differently to wage hikes than small and medium-sized businesses.
Some longitudinal studies indicate initial shocks to employment levels can level off over time as the market adjusts.
